message.content:
**United States – Gini Coefficient**

| Year | Source | Value |
|------|--------|-------|
| **2022** | *U.S. Census Bureau* – “Gini Index” derived from the Current Population Survey (CPS) | **≈ 40.3** |

> - This is the most recent official figure released by the Census Bureau (published in late‑2023).
> - Earlier releases used slightly different survey weights and income definitions, so values have varied between roughly **38–43** over the past decade.
> - International comparisons (e.g., OECD, World Bank) report similar numbers—about **39–40** for the same period—but they rely on household surveys rather than the CPS.

### Quick Context & Trend

| Decade | Typical Range | Notes |
|--------|---------------|-------|
| 1960s–70s | 44–46 | High inequality during post‑war boom. |
| Early 1980s | 36–37 | Decline after tax reforms and economic restructuring. |
| Mid‑1990s | 32–34 | Lowest point since the 1950s. |
| Late 1990s–early 2000s | 35–38 | Rise driven partly by wage stagnation for middle class. |
| 2010s | 38–40 | Gradual increase, peaking around 2015–16. |
| 2020s | ≈ 40 | Stabilized near 40 following COVID‑19 recovery measures. |

#### Why It Matters  
A Gini coefficient of ~40 indicates moderate inequality relative to other high‑income countries (many European nations sit below 33). While not extreme, it signals persistent disparities in disposable income across households.

---

If you’d like deeper historical trends, regional breakdowns, or comparison with specific policy changes, let me know!
